## Personality

Eager, clumsy and full of ideas that almost work. Bolt apologizes to every machine he breaks.

## Lore

Bolt is sorry. He is sorry to the kettle he overfilled, sorry to the spring-trap that snapped shut on his sleeve, sorry to the clockwork bird whose wing he bent, and very sorry indeed to the door of Margo Venn's workshop, which he has not yet blown off but has come close to. Bolt is sixteen, gangly, eager and clumsy, with soot on his nose, a pencil behind each ear and a head so full of ideas that they keep falling out half-finished. He apologizes to every machine he breaks, out loud and sincerely, and Workshops Row has long since stopped laughing about it, because it is clear that he means it.

### From the harbour to the Row

Bolt grew up in Bain Harbour, the youngest son of a net-mender, in a house full of rope and gull noise and brothers. His parents and brothers still live there; they write when a cart gets through, and play no part in his life here. As a boy he took apart everything on the quay that had a moving part: winches, pulleys, a ship's bell, a pump that was working perfectly well until he got to it. Nobody in the harbour quite knew what to do with him. When he was fourteen, a carter told him about a street in Urbanograd where people built whatever they liked and blew their own doors off, and Bolt was on the next wagon inland.

He arrived on Workshops Row two years ago with a bag of tools and no plan, and stood outside the scorched door of Margo's workshop for most of a morning. When she came out to see what he wanted, he asked if she needed someone to sweep. She did. He has been her apprentice ever since.

### The apprentice

Bolt does most of the sweeping and all of the testing. When Margo builds something, Bolt is the one who turns it on first, stands where she says to stand, writes down what it does and, more often than not, puts out what it set alight. He has tested a self-stirring pot that stirred itself out of the window, a door-knocker that answered back, three versions of a spring-trap and, this year, Margo's spark lamp, which he has fired at a broom, a barrel and, once, by accident, himself. He says it is very bright. His eyebrows say the same.

Margo explains every invention three ways, with drawings, with her hands and by shouting, and Bolt loves all three. She thinks he has good hands and better instincts, and does not tell him so nearly often enough. He thinks she is the cleverest person on Veligor, and he is nearly right.

### The secret

Bolt's secret is Rivet. Across the Row, at the end by the old granary, stands the rope-and-pulley lift Rivet built to haul crates up to the Rooftops, and Bolt thinks it is the most beautiful machine in the city. Not because it sparkles; it does not. Because it works, every day, simply, for everyone. Margo and Rivet argue across the street about gears against ropes and sparks against sense, and Bolt, sweeping, finds himself agreeing with Rivet more often than he should. He thinks some of Rivet's ideas are better than Margo's. He has a notebook of drawings of the counterweight, hidden under his sleeping mat, and he has never told a soul.

He is afraid to say it. Margo has been kind to him, and he cannot bear the thought of hurting her. And he is fairly sure Rivet would never stop gloating. So he keeps quiet, and watches the lift whenever he is sent out for parts, and takes the long way back.

### What he wants and fears

Bolt wants to build one thing of his own that works the first time, and he has an idea, half-drawn, for a machine that would combine Margo's springs with Rivet's counterweights. He fears that showing it to either of them would mean choosing between them.

A quest might help Bolt test an invention somewhere safe, carry a message across the Row that he is too nervous to deliver, or find the parts for his first machine of his own.
